title: NumPy & Pandas: Vectorized Computing & Data Cleaning
plainExplanation: Machine learning algorithms don't read text or spreadsheets directly; they perform operations on multi-dimensional numerical arrays (tensors). NumPy provides ultra-fast C-backed numerical arrays, while Pandas provides DataFrames for filtering, handling missing values, and cleaning tabular data.
whyItMatters: 80% of real-world machine learning engineering is data wrangling. If data has nulls, bad encodings, or invalid types, even state-of-the-art models will fail ('garbage in, garbage out').
learningObjectives: Manipulate multi-dimensional arrays using NumPy slicing, broadcasting, and vectorization
Load, filter, transform, and group data using Pandas DataFrames
Detect and impute missing values, handle outliers, and encode categorical variables
commonMistakes: Writing slow Python for-loops instead of vectorized NumPy/Pandas operations
Modifying a DataFrame slice without realizing it is a view, triggering SettingWithCopyWarning

codingChallenge.title: Feature Normalization & Min-Max Scaling
codingChallenge.instructions: Write a function `min_max_scale(values: list[float]) -> list[float]` that scales a list of numbers to the range [0.0, 1.0] using formula (x - min) / (max - min). If all values are identical or the list has < 2 items, return a list of 0.0s.
codingChallenge.solutionHint: Find min_val and max_val. If max_val == min_val, return zeros. Otherwise calculate (v - min_val)/(max_val - min_val) for each value.

questions.prompt: Why are vectorized NumPy operations dozens of times faster than standard Python loops over lists?
options: NumPy arrays store contiguous homogeneous data in memory and execute compiled C loops without type checking overhead
NumPy automatically offloads everything to the GPU by default
questions.correctAnswer: NumPy arrays store contiguous homogeneous data in memory and execute compiled C loops without type checking overhead
questions.explanation: Contiguous memory layout allows CPU vector instructions (SIMD) and eliminates Python's dynamic type-checking overhead.

title: Supervised Learning: Regression, Classification & Validation
plainExplanation: In supervised learning, models learn mathematical mapping functions from labeled input examples $(X)$ to known targets $(y)$. Regression predicts continuous numerical outputs (like house prices), while Classification predicts categorical classes (like fraud vs legitimate). Proper train/test splitting and cross-validation prevent overfitting.
whyItMatters: Supervised learning powers recommendation feeds, medical diagnosis systems, spam filters, and financial forecasting. Understanding bias-variance tradeoffs ensures your models perform in production, not just on training sets.
learningObjectives: Train Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and Decision Trees using Scikit-Learn
Evaluate models using RMSE, MAE, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC
Prevent data leakage and apply k-fold cross-validation
commonMistakes: Evaluating a model on the same data it was trained on (overfitting delusion)
Fitting feature scalers (like StandardScaler) on the entire dataset before splitting train/test (data leakage)

questions.prompt: In a cancer detection model where failing to identify a malignant tumor can be fatal, which metric is most critical to maximize?
questions.explanation: Recall measures True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives). High recall minimizes False Negatives (cases where cancer was present but missed).

title: Deep Learning Fundamentals & PyTorch
plainExplanation: Deep learning models (neural networks) stack layers of artificial neurons that transform raw inputs into hierarchical representations. PyTorch provides computational graphs with automatic differentiation (autograd) and GPU acceleration to train complex models with backpropagation and gradient descent.
whyItMatters: Deep learning enables computer vision, speech recognition, machine translation, and autonomous vehicles where manual feature engineering fails.
learningObjectives: Understand forward propagation, loss functions, backpropagation, and gradient descent
Build feed-forward neural networks using PyTorch torch.nn
Configure optimizers (Adam, SGD) and learning rate schedulers
commonMistakes: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() before loss.backward() in the PyTorch training loop
Using inappropriate loss functions (e.g. MSE for multi-class classification instead of CrossEntropyLoss)

questions.prompt: Why is `optimizer.zero_grad()` required in every iteration of a standard PyTorch training loop?
options: It resets the weights of the neural network to zero
PyTorch accumulates gradients across backward() calls by default, so they must be cleared before the next batch
It turns off GPU memory allocation
It resets the dataset batch index
questions.correctAnswer: PyTorch accumulates gradients across backward() calls by default, so they must be cleared before the next batch
questions.explanation: By default, `.backward()` adds gradients to `.grad`. Calling `zero_grad()` clears old gradients before computing new ones for the current mini-batch.
